Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative primarily unfolds as a real-time scene—following Ilse's ferry crossing from departure to arrival—using vivid sensory details (the singing steel cable, the fog, the vibrating phone on metal) and sparse, realistic dialogue to engage the reader and build quiet tension. At the same time, the writer weaves in brief moments of exposition and summary (such as Ilse's decades of experience on the river and the background of the young female student) to provide context and depth without interrupting the pacing or pulling the reader out of the immediate moment.
